x.ASV: Send ye the lambs for the ruler of the land from Selah to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion.
x.Darby: Send the lamb of the ruler of the land from the rock to the wilderness, — unto the mount of the daughter of Zion.
x.KJV: Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion.
x.YLT: Send ye a lamb to the ruler of the land, From Selah in the wilderness, Unto the mount of the daughter of Zion.

nt: Isaiah is speaking as if the city of Zion were a person, referring to it as **the daughter of Zion**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Zion]

x.ASV: For it shall be that, as wandering birds, as a scattered nest, so shall the daughters of Moab be at the fords of the Arnon.
x.Darby: And it shall be [that] as a wandering bird, [as] a scattered nest, so shall the daughters of Moab be at the fords of the Arnon.
x.KJV: For it shall be, that, as a wandering bird cast out of the nest, so the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon.
x.YLT: And it hath come to pass, As a wandering bird, a nest cast out, Are daughters of Moab, at fords of Arnon.

nt: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **And it will happen** to introduce a new event. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The point of this comparison is that just as **a wandering bird scattered from a nest** is displaced and helpless, so **the daughters of Moab** will be displaced and vulnerable **at the fords of the Arnon**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a helpless, wandering bird scattered from a nest]

The expression **scattered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that someone drove from a nest]

x.ASV: Give counsel, execute justice; make thy shade as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; betray not the fugitive.
x.Darby: Bring in counsel, execute justice; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of noonday; hide the outcasts, discover not the fugitive.
x.KJV: Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth.
x.YLT: Bring ye in counsel, do judgment, Make as night thy shadow in the midst of noon, Hide outcasts, the wanderer reveal not.

nt: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please bring counsel and do justice]

The point of this comparison is that just as **night** provides deep darkness and concealment, so the Moabites are asking Judah to provide a **shadow** that completely hides them at **noon**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Make your shadow conceal us as completely as the darkness of night conceals, even in the brightest part of the day]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **counsel** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Bring wise advice, do what is right]

These two phrases express the same idea. The first states it positively as a request to **hide**, and the second states it negatively as a request not to **reveal**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine these phrases. Alternate translation: [Please hide the outcast ones and do not tell anyone where they have gone]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hide the outcast ones]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not tell anyone where the wanderer has gone]

t: he will come to an end

x.ASV: Let mine outcasts dwell with thee; as for Moab, be thou a covert to him from the face of the destroyer. For the extortioner is brought to nought, destruction ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land.
x.Darby: Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the waster. For the extortioner is at an end, the wasting hath ceased, the oppressors are consumed out of the land.
x.KJV: Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land.
x.YLT: Sojourn in thee do My outcasts, O Moab, Be a secret hiding-place to them, From the face of a destroyer, For ceased hath the extortioner, Finished hath been a destroyer, Consumed the treaders down out of the land.

nt: The leaders of Moab are saying what they want the ruler of Judah to allow the outcast ones of Moab to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Allow the outcast ones of Moab to live among you]

Isaiah is using the adjective **outcast** as a noun to mean people who have been driven from their homes. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who have been cast out of]

The leaders of Moab are speaking as if the protection they are requesting were a physical **shelter**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be a place of refuge for them]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be a shelter for them]

Here, **the face of** represents the presence of **the destroyer**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of the destroyer]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the destroying]

x.ASV: And a throne shall be established in lovingkindness; and one shall sit thereon in truth, in the tent of David, judging, and seeking justice, and swift to do righteousness.
x.Darby: And a throne shall be established in mercy: and in the tent of David there shall sit upon it, in truth, one judging and seeking justice and hastening righteousness.
x.KJV: And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness.
x.YLT: And established in kindness is the throne, And one hath sat on it in truth, in the tent of David, Judging and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness.

nt: Here, **the throne** represents the royal authority and reign of the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the royal authority will be established]

The expression **will be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will establish the throne]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [keeping covenant promises]
The word **one** refers to a future ruler from the line of David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and a future ruler from the line of David will sit on it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [truly]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the Davidic dynasty were a physical **tent** that one could sit in. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in David’s dynasty]

The phrase **judging and seeking justice** expresses a single idea. The words **seeking justice** tell more about **judging**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [judging justly]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is just and quickly doing right]

x.ASV: We have heard of the pride of Moab, that he is very proud; even of his arrogancy, and his pride, and his wrath; his boastings are nought.
x.Darby: We have heard of the arrogance of Moab, — [he is] very proud, — of his pride, and his arrogance, and his wrath: his pratings are vain.
x.KJV: We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is very proud: even of his haughtiness, and his pride, and his wrath: but his lies shall not be so.
x.YLT: We have heard of the pride of Moab--very proud, His pride, and his arrogance, and his wrath, Not right are his devices.

nt: The terms **arrogance** and **pride** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [its great arrogance and its overflow]

The phrases **its arrogance and its pride** and **its overflow** together express a single idea. The term **overflow** tells more about the **arrogance** and **pride** (that is, the great pride) of the Moabites. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [its overflowingly great arrogance]

x.ASV: Therefore shall Moab wail for Moab, every one shall wail: for the raisin-cakes of Kir-hareseth shall ye mourn, utterly stricken.
x.Darby: Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab; every one of them shall howl. For the foundations of Kirhareseth shall ye mourn, verily afflicted.
x.KJV: Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl: for the foundations of Kir–hareseth shall ye mourn; surely they are stricken.
x.YLT: Therefore howl doth Moab for Moab, all of it doth howl, For the grape-cakes of Kir-Hareseth it meditateth, Surely they are smitten.

nt: The word **Therefore** introduces a result of Moab’s pride described in the previous verse. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Because of their pride,]

Isaiah is speaking of **Moab** as if it were a living thing that could **wail**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Moab will wail over their land]

The term **raisin cakes** refers to a kind of dried-fruit food made from pressed grapes. If your readers would not be familiar with what raisin cakes are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the dried-fruit treats of Kir Hareseth]

The expression **stricken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they will grieve]

x.ASV: For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have broken down the choice branches thereof, which reached even unto Jazer, which wandered into the wilderness; its shoots were spread abroad, they passed over the sea.
x.Darby: For the fields of Heshbon languish, the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have broken down its choice plants: they reached unto Jaazer, they wandered [through] the wilderness; its shoots stretched out, they went beyond the sea.
x.KJV: For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah: the lords of the heathen have broken down the principal plants thereof, they are come even unto Jazer, they wandered through the wilderness: her branches are stretched out, they are gone over the sea.
x.YLT: Because fields of Heshbon languish, The vine of Sibmah, Lords of nations did beat her choice vines, Unto Jazer they have come, They have wandered in a wilderness, Her plants have spread themselves, They have passed over a sea.

nt: Isaiah is speaking of **the fields of Heshbon** as if they were a living thing that could be **enfeebled**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the crops in the fields of Heshbon have failed]

Isaiah is speaking as if Sibmah’s valuable resources were **choice vines** that could be stomped. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [its finest crops]
The pronoun **They** refers to the choice vines of Sibmah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [They, the vines, reached to Jazer]
The pronoun **its** refers to the vine of Sibmah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the shoots of Sibmah’s vine spread out]
עַד־יַעְזֵ֥ר נָגָ֖עוּ תָּ֣עוּ מִדְבָּ֑ר שְׁלֻ֣חוֹתֶ֔י⁠הָ נִטְּשׁ֖וּ עָ֥בְרוּ יָֽם

Isaiah is speaking of **the vines** and **shoots** as if they were living things that could **reach**, **wander**, **spread out**, and **pass on**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The vines extended to Jazer, they spread {into} the wilderness; its shoots spread out, they reached {to} the sea]

x.ASV: Therefore I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh: for upon thy summer fruits and upon thy harvest the battle shout is fallen.
x.Darby: Therefore I will weep with the weeping of Jaazer for the vine of Sibmah; with my tears will I water thee, Heshbon, and Elealeh, for a cry is fallen upon thy summer fruits and upon thy harvest.
x.KJV: Therefore I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer the vine of Sibmah: I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh: for the shouting for thy summer fruits and for thy harvest is fallen.
x.YLT: Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer, The vine of Sibmah, I water thee with my tear, O Heshbon and Elealeh, For--for thy summer fruits, and for thy harvest, The shouting hath fallen.

nt: Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. See the UST. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

Isaiah is speaking to the cities of **Heshbon and Elealeh** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the devastation of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Heshbon and Elealeh. Alternate translation: [I will shed many tears for Heshbon and Elealeh]

Isaiah says **I will drench you with my tears** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [I will weep many tears for you]

Isaiah is speaking of **shouting** as if it were a living thing that could **fall**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the shouting has stopped]

x.ASV: And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the fruitful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither joyful noise: no treader shall tread out wine in the presses; I have made the vintage shout to cease.
x.Darby: And joy and gladness is taken away out of the fruitful field; and in the vineyards there is no singing, neither is there shouting: the treaders tread out no wine in the presses, I have made the cry [of the winepress] to cease.
x.KJV: And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting: the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease.
x.YLT: And removed have been gladness and joy from the fruitful field, And in vineyards they sing not, nor shout, Wine in the presses treadeth not the treader, Shouting I have caused to cease.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **gladness** and **rejoicing**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [And no one feels glad anymore, and no one rejoices in the agricultural land]

The expression **is gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And gladness has departed]

The expression **it is not sung** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [one does not sing]

Isaiah is using the word **one** in a general sense, not to refer to a specific person. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one shouts joyfully]

x.ASV: Wherefore my heart soundeth like a harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kir-heres.
x.Darby: Therefore my bowels sound like a harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kirheres.
x.KJV: Wherefore my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kir–haresh.
x.YLT: Therefore my bowels for Moab as a harp do sound, And mine inward parts for Kir-Haresh.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **a harp** produces a sustained, mournful sound, so Isaiah’s **insides moan** deeply and continuously for the suffering of **Moab**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [my insides moan deeply and continuously for Moab]
עַל־כֵּן֙ מֵעַ֣⁠י לְ⁠מוֹאָ֔ב כַּ⁠כִּנּ֖וֹר יֶֽהֱמ֑וּ וְ⁠קִרְבִּ֖⁠י לְ⁠קִ֥יר חָֽרֶשׂ

Isaiah is speaking of his **insides**, his **inward part**, as if it were a living thing that could **moan like a harp**, that is, play a sad tune on a harp. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I feel so badly that it is as if my insides are playing a sad tune for Moab. Yes, it is as if my inward part is doing that for Kir Heres]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and my inward part moans for Kir Heres]

x.ASV: And it shall come to pass, when Moab presenteth himself, when he wearieth himself upon the high place, and shall come to his sanctuary to pray, that he shall not prevail.
x.Darby: And it shall come to pass, when Moab shall appear, shall weary himself on the high place, and enter into his sanctuary to pray, that he shall not prevail.
x.KJV: And it shall come to pass, when it is seen that Moab is weary on the high place, that he shall come to his sanctuary to pray; but he shall not prevail.
x.YLT: And it hath come to pass, when it hath been seen, That weary hath been Moab on the high place, And he hath come unto his sanctuary to pray, And is not able.

nt: וְ⁠הָיָ֧ה כִֽי־נִרְאָ֛ה כִּֽי־נִלְאָ֥ה מוֹאָ֖ב עַל־הַ⁠בָּמָ֑ה וּ⁠בָ֧א אֶל־מִקְדָּשׁ֛⁠וֹ לְ⁠הִתְפַּלֵּ֖ל וְ⁠לֹ֥א יוּכָֽל

Here, **to pray** marks praying as the goal or purpose of coming to the sanctuary. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [And it will happen, when it is seen that Moab is wearied on the high place, that it will come to its sanctuary for the purpose of praying, but it will not be able]
See how you translated the similar expression in [16:2](../16/02.md).

The expression **it is seen** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when everyone sees]

The implication is that **the high place** is a site for pagan worship. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [is wearied on the high place, a site for pagan worship]

The expression **is wearied** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Moab has worn itself out]
The pronoun **it** refers to the nation of Moab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Moab will come to their sanctuary]

Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between Moab coming to its sanctuary to pray and its inability to accomplish anything by praying. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, it will not be able.]

x.ASV: This is the word that Jehovah spake concerning Moab in time past.
x.Darby: This is the word which Jehovah hath spoken from of old concerning Moab.
x.KJV: This is the word that the Lord hath spoken concerning Moab since that time.
x.YLT: This is the word that Jehovah hath spoken unto Moab from that time,

nt: Isaiah is using the term **word** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. This refers to all he said in [15:1](../15/01.md)–[16:12](../16/12.md). If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This is the message]

t: and/ it will be lightly esteemed

x.ASV: But now Jehovah hath spoken, saying, Within three years, as the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab shall be brought into contempt, with all his great multitude; and the remnant shall be very small and of no account.
x.Darby: And now Jehovah speaketh saying, Within three years, as the years of a hired servant, and the glory of Moab shall be brought to nothing, with all that great multitude; and the remnant shall be small, few, of no account.
x.KJV: But now the Lord hath spoken, saying, Within three years, as the years of an hireling, and the glory of Moab shall be contemned, with all that great multitude; and the remnant shall be very small and feeble.
x.YLT: And now hath Jehovah spoken, saying, `In three years, as years of an hireling, Lightly esteemed is the honour of Moab, With all the great multitude, And the remnant is little, small, not mighty!'

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **the years of a hired one** are counted precisely because the worker tracks every day of the contract, so the **three years** until Moab’s downfall will be measured exactly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [which a person hired to work under contract counts very carefully]

Here **the glory of Moab** represents the nation’s honored status and reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Moab’s honored status]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [glorious Moab]

The expression **will be despised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will treat the glory of Moab with contempt]

Yahweh is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. By saying the remnant will be **not mighty**, he means they will be very weak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [very weak]
